Emerging Compounders|U|Universe: Connor Haley states that leaving out commodity sectors means searching where lasting advantages are more common, because his team found energy, materials and financials rarely contain many businesses with real competitive edges. A mentioned example: Alta Fox's study of 104 multibaggers (2015-2020) excluded energy, materials and financials from the start. Terry Smith states that avoiding materials means avoiding a sector with persistently low returns, because returns on capital stay in place for decades and a low price does not turn a bad company into a good one. A mentioned example: in his sector data, materials sat with utilities, telecoms, transport, energy and retailing among the persistently low-return groups.
Emerging Compounders|E1|History: No investor source: you need a few years of numbers before growth and margin trends can be measured at all.
Emerging Compounders|E2|Recent report: No investor source: a data-quality rule, because old annual numbers can hide a recent collapse.
Emerging Compounders|E3|Already profitab: Connor Haley states that already having positive EBITDA means the company is a proven business, not a cash burner, because most big winners were past the profit turning point and were not losing money and diluting shareholders to survive. A mentioned example: in Alta Fox's study of 104 multibaggers (2015-2020), 88% already had positive EBITDA five years earlier.
Emerging Compounders|E4|Fast growth: Connor Haley states that fast revenue growth means the company has the engine multibaggers need, because the big winners were growth businesses whose rising sales and profits got the market to re-rate them. A mentioned example: in Alta Fox's 104-stock study the median winner grew revenue 21% a year and EBITDA 28%; even the 25th percentile grew revenue 14% a year.
Emerging Compounders|E5|Growth not fadin: Alex Sacerdote states that growth still running today means the main risk is not playing out, because "the biggest reason people blow up in tech is they miss on revenue". A mentioned example: US electric-car adoption stalled near 10%, so Whale Rock's rating of that S-curve fell from 10 out of 10 to zero and it stopped owning Tesla.
Emerging Compounders|E6|Gross margin: Connor Haley states that a healthy gross margin means there is room for profit to grow faster than sales, because a company needs enough gross profit on each sale before spreading fixed costs can lift its margins. A mentioned example: in Alta Fox's study, the median multibagger had gross margins in the mid-40s% and EBITDA margins just over 10% at the start.
Emerging Compounders|E7|Operating levera: Connor Haley states that overhead falling as a share of sales means the company is reaching operating leverage, because costs growing slower than revenue lift margins, which is often when an undiscovered stock gets re-rated. A mentioned example: in Alta Fox's study, the median winner's SG&A fell 416 basis points of revenue and its EBITDA margin rose 753 basis points over five years. Alex Sacerdote states that rising margins on top of fast growth mean earnings can grow much faster than sales, because with S-curve adoption and a rising margin "your earnings don't grow linearly they grow exponentially". A mentioned example: Whale Rock bought Tesla around end-2019 and 2020, when a cheaper Model 3 made electric-car adoption take off.
Emerging Compounders|E8|Little dilution: Connor Haley states that little dilution means growth reaches each existing share, because per-share value matters more than size, and the big winners were funding themselves instead of issuing stock to cover losses. A mentioned example: in Alta Fox's 104-stock study, the winners were proven concepts that were not losing millions and meaningfully diluting shareholders. Chris Davis states that a share count that does not rise means value builds up for each owner, because long-term compounding only reaches holders if the company is not handing out more slices of itself. A mentioned example: his 50-year study found lasting winners such as Exxon and Philip Morris tended to have share counts that did not go up.
Emerging Compounders|E9|Leverage: Connor Haley states that modest debt means downside protection, because a strong balance sheet lets a small company get through a shock that could push a levered one toward bankruptcy. A mentioned example: in March 2020 Alta Fox sold a well-run restaurant stock that had just borrowed to buy another business right before COVID. Brian Gaines states that heavy debt turns the equity into "an option bet", because lenders, especially banks, can force a levered company into bankruptcy, so the share price no longer tracks business value. A mentioned example: Movie Gallery, with $1.1 billion of debt on about 30 million shares, which he described as an option bet.
Emerging Compounders|E10|Size (market ca: Connor Haley states that a minimum size means avoiding the tiniest stocks, because Alta Fox's preference for high-quality businesses has worked better a bit higher up, where it has done much better in small, mid and large caps. A mentioned example: Alta Fox's worst market-cap bucket since inception has been micro caps, and its multibagger study only counted companies above $150M.
Emerging Compounders|E11|Not already lar: Connor Haley states that staying below about $10B means the company still has room to multiply, because Alta Fox likes small caps that grow into mid caps and mid caps that grow into large caps, and that growth drives the return. A mentioned example: Alta Fox's study of 104 multibaggers only looked at companies with market caps between $150M and $10B.
Emerging Compounders|E12|Valuation: Connor Haley states that a moderate EV/EBITDA means the thesis can work on profit growth alone, because "if your entire thesis rests on significant multiple expansion maybe it's not a great thesis". A mentioned example: in his study the median multibagger traded about 10x forward EBITDA five years earlier and re-rated to about 25x, with two-thirds of the return from multiple expansion. Chris Davis states that a reasonable starting multiple means your return is set by the business, because he assumes no re-rating: "We may get it, but it's nowhere in our models." A mentioned example: in 2026 his holdings at about 14x earnings offered a 7.5% earnings yield, versus about 3.8% for the market at 26x.
Emerging Compounders|E13|Liquidity: Connor Haley states that trading of at least $200k a day means a stock is "reasonably liquid" for a small and micro cap investor, because a fund has to be able to build and exit a real position. A mentioned example: Alta Fox's 104-multibagger study used average daily value traded over $200k as an entry filter.
Emerging Compounders|J|Human / AI review: Connor Haley states that the questions numbers miss decide the case, because "why might this stock be mispriced" is the key question, 70% customer concentration is a risk that never goes away, and small-cap managers should own at least about 5%. A mentioned example: XPEL, a focused niche leader that competes with far bigger 3M, which he says a focused player can often out-innovate. Pat Dorsey states that moat strength needs human research, because "you can't screen for switching costs"; you have to talk to customers and others who know the business. No specific past example given.
Special Situations|U|Universe (event): Joel Greenblatt states that spin-offs and post-bankruptcy stocks mean likely mispricing, because analysts stop covering a messy company "until the smoke is cleared", and lenders handed shares in a bankruptcy usually sell them. A mentioned example: his Sears stub, bought for about $5 in 1993, reached $30 in two months. Connor Haley states that spin-offs, post-bankruptcy firms and recent IPOs mean a possible edge, because the market has not had long to analyze them, so they can stay mispriced. No specific past example given.
Special Situations|S1|Recent report: No investor source: a data-quality rule, because you need current filed numbers to judge the business.
Special Situations|S2|Profitable busines: Joel Greenblatt states that real operating profit means you can judge whether the business is both good and cheap, because he measures stocks on EBIT against enterprise value and against capital, looking for high returns bought at a high earnings yield. A mentioned example: NII Holdings, a post-bankruptcy wireless business at 2.8x EBITDA, went from $10 to $240 split-adjusted.
Special Situations|S3|Leverage: Brian Gaines states that heavy debt turns the equity into "an option bet", because the capital structure decides whether a company can be pushed into bankruptcy: banks can force it, while fixed-rate bondholders cannot. A mentioned example: Movie Gallery, with $1.1 billion of debt on about 30 million shares, which he said had become an option bet whose share price meant little.
Special Situations|S4|Cheap: Joel Greenblatt states that a low EV/EBIT means you are paid well for the risk, because he thinks in pre-tax multiples against a bond yield of at least 6%: about 10x EBIT is similar to that yield, and 12x needs real certainty. A mentioned example: he warned students who put 12x EBIT on their write-ups that only a pretty good business deserves it.
Special Situations|S5|Size (market cap): No investor source: a tradeability rule, because very small companies are hard to buy without moving the price.
Special Situations|S6|Liquidity: No investor source: a tradeability rule, because you must be able to get in and out of the stock.
Special Situations|J|Human / AI review: Joel Greenblatt states that you must read why the parent is acting and how managers are paid, because many spin-offs come from a position of weakness, and stock owned versus yearly pay is the main thing he checks on management. A mentioned example: when Sears said it had no intention of disposing of Allstate, he read it as a sign it would. Brian Gaines states that insiders putting more money in means the business is not falling apart, because they know more than outsiders do. A mentioned example: Hollywood Video's CEO Mark Wattles rolled his stake into a buyout, going from about 10% to 50% ownership. Chris Davis states that hidden assets and senior claims change the real price, because you should value the whole company like a buyer, counting debt and pensions and assets carried below value. No specific past example given.
Cyclicals|U|Universe: Stanley Druckenmiller states that capacity-cycle industries need cycle-aware rules, because when companies lose money capacity shrinks and margins recover within about three years, while flush industries announce expansions that bring margins down. A mentioned example: chemicals, his early sector, where you bought when everyone was losing money and shutting capacity. Connor Haley states that a cyclical company must be judged on trough numbers, because its profits swing with the cycle, so he wants it at a trough multiple on trough margins. No specific past example given.
Cyclicals|C1|History: Joel Greenblatt states that a long record means you can see the bad years and find normal earnings, because good and bad years must be averaged: $10 a year for nine years plus one break-even year is about $9. A mentioned example: Wells Fargo could earn about $18 a share in a normal year yet roughly zero once every seven or eight years.
Cyclicals|C2|Recent report: No investor source: a data-quality rule, because old annual numbers can hide a recent collapse.
Cyclicals|C3|Size (revenue): No investor source: a data and ownership rule, because tiny filers have patchier numbers and are hard to own.
Cyclicals|C4|Mid-cycle returns: Chris Davis states that solid returns on capital mean the business, not the entry price, drives a long-term owner's return, because "your return over time is going to approach the return on equity of the business, no matter what your starting price is." A mentioned example: buy a business at half of book that keeps reinvesting at 4%, and your return heads toward 4%. Terry Smith states that a good return record means a good business, because returns on capital stay persistent for decades and a low rating does not turn a bad company into a good one. A mentioned example: in his sector data, transport, energy and materials stayed persistently low-return groups.
Cyclicals|C5|Survives downturns: Joel Greenblatt states that staying profitable in bad years means a cyclical is worth more than its swings suggest, because a business that does not lose money in a bust keeps its earning power and survives. A mentioned example: NVR, a homebuilder with pre-sold homes and little capital tied up, which in a downturn might take a small hit but probably would not lose money.
Cyclicals|C6|Leverage: Joel Greenblatt states that low debt matters most in cyclicals, because whether a company survives the cycle depends on how leveraged it is, and you don't want to lever up a very cyclical business. No specific past example given. Brian Gaines states that heavy debt turns the equity into "an option bet", because banks can force a levered company into bankruptcy in a bad stretch. A mentioned example: Movie Gallery, with $1.1 billion of debt on about 30 million shares. Connor Haley states that a strong balance sheet means downside protection, because it lets a company survive a shock. A mentioned example: in March 2020 Alta Fox sold a restaurant stock that had just borrowed for an acquisition before COVID.
Cyclicals|C7|Not at peak margins: Stanley Druckenmiller states that buying when margins are low means buying before the recovery, because "when companies are losing money, capacity is always going to shrink and their margins going to look better in 3 years", while over-earners' margins come down. A mentioned example: in 2022 he named ocean shipping, with "massive margins", among the true over-earners, after retail and trucking. Connor Haley states that a cyclical should be bought at trough margins, because buying near peak margins means buying profits that will shrink. No specific past example given.
Cyclicals|C8|Cheap on normalized earning: Joel Greenblatt states that a low price on cycle-average earnings means a real bargain, because he draws the normal earnings line through good and bad years and pays a low multiple on it, instead of trusting one year. A mentioned example: Wells Fargo, with normalized earnings near $16 a share at about $70, dipped to $60 and later reached $250. Connor Haley states that a cyclical should trade at a trough multiple on trough margins, because then the price already assumes the bad part of the cycle. No specific past example given.
Cyclicals|J|Human / AI review: Stanley Druckenmiller states that the capacity picture tells you where margins go next, because industries shutting capacity recover while flush ones announcing expansions show you what is coming. A mentioned example: in chemicals, companies used to announce capacity expansions at the peak, "so you knew what was going to happen." Joel Greenblatt states that the key question for a cheap, troubled stock is whether its problem is temporary or permanent, because only a temporary problem makes the low price a bargain. A mentioned example: Rich Pzena's case for Lear, the auto supplier, rested on showing its problem was short-term.
